info.bio:
Jerry Lee Lewis (nacido el 29 de septiembre de 1935) es un pianista y cantante pionero del rock and roll estadounidense.

Nació en Ferriday, Louisiana. Pronto mostró un talento natural al piano. Aunque pobres, sus padres hipotecaron la casa para comprarle un piano. Al igual que Elvis Presley, creció cantando música gospel en las iglesias pentecostales del sur. Empezó a tocar el piano a muy temprana edad en su iglesia, y en 1950 empezó a asistir a una escuela de lectura de la biblia de Texas

scenes.name: Rock'n'roll
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Fusión de rhythm'n'blues y country, con mucho más peso del primero. Chuck Berry inventa en 1955 el rock'n'roll tal como se conocerá durante cincuenta años (la guitarra como instrumento protagonista, canciones propias que hablan a los adolescentes); Bo Diddley aporta el ritmo «hambone», Little Richard y Esquerita el histerismo y el maquillaje (el primer «decadence-rock»), Jerry Lee Lewis el piano feroz y Sun Records el rockabilly. Elvis Presley es, para Scaruffi, «la primera gran estafa del rock'n'roll». Buddy Holly y Eddie Cochran abren otra vía; en paralelo nacen el soul (Ray Charles), la exótica (Martin Denny, Esquivel), la música electrónica de cinta y, en Gran Bretaña, el skiffle.

podcast.title: Discovery and Early Recordings (1956)
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis was discovered by Sam Phillips' assistant, Cowboy Jack Clement, in November 1956. He cut his first record for Sun Records a couple of weeks before the December 4, 1956 session, and that first record was released three days prior to that session. "Jerry Lee Lewis was a new piano player, who had been discovered by Sam Phillips as assistant, Cowboy Jack Clement, the previous month."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Session Musician for Christmas Presents (1956)
podcast.body: On December 4, 1956, Jerry Lee Lewis participated in Carl Perkins' recording session for "Matchbox" not as a primary performer, but as a session musician. His motivation was to earn enough money to buy Christmas presents for his parents. "but he was just working as a session musician, trying to earn enough money to buy his parents some Christmas presents, by sitting in on the session."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: "The Return of Jerry Lee" Single (1958)
podcast.body: In an attempt by Sun Records to both capitalize on and defuse the controversy surrounding Jerry Lee Lewis's scandalous marriage, Jack Clement produced a novelty record. This single, a joke initially for Sun staff, featured DJ George Klein interviewing Lewis about the controversy, with Lewis's answers spliced from his existing records. Sam Phillips, despite its origins as a joke, insisted on releasing it. However, the record, which included "leering jokes about Myra's physical attractiveness," failed to defuse the situation and was criticized for its exploitation of a child. "Unsurprisingly, that did not have the effect that was hoped, and did not defuse the situation one Iota."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: 1958 Tour Co-Headliner with Chuck Berry
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis co-headlined a 1958 tour with Chuck Berry, featuring Alan Fried as the MC. Despite initial tension between the two stars, the shared adversity of the Boston concert incident brought them closer, leading them to become close friends who spoke highly of each other. "In the last couple of episodes I've mentioned a tour that Chuck Berry and Jerry Lee Lewis headlined in 1958, just after Johnny Be Good came out, with Alan Fried as the MC."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 67: "Johnny B. Goode", by Chuck Berry

podcast.title: Scandalous Marriage and UK Tour Downfall (1958)
podcast.body: On May 21, 1958, during what was meant to be a triumphant UK tour, Jerry Lee Lewis's career collapsed when the press discovered he had married his 13-year-old cousin, Myra Gale Brown. This revelation, made public upon their arrival in the UK, immediately halted the tour, which was meant to last six weeks but ended after just three days. Lewis's actions, involving a 20-something man marrying a 13-year-old in his own family, were unequivocally deemed "child sexual abuse" and "simply wrong." While Lewis and those around him did not view it as wrong within the context of the Southern US culture at the time, where young marriages to older men were common, this cultural context does not excuse his behavior. His own bass player and Myra's father, J.W. Brown, was so enraged he attempted to murder Lewis with a shotgun, only being deterred by Sam Phillips. "And that is when everything came crashing down, because it was when he and his entourage landed in the UK and the press saw the 13-year-old girl with him and asked who she was that it became public knowledge he had married his 13-year-old cousin, Maver."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: "Breathless" Promotional Scheme
podcast.body: Judd Phillips, Sam Phillips' brother, devised a unique promotional campaign for "Breathless" in conjunction with Dick Clark, who hosted "The Dick Clark Show" (also known as "Dick Clark's Saturday Night Beach Nut Show," sponsored by Beach Nut Chewing Gum). Fans could send Sun Records five Beach Nut wrappers and 50 cents for postage and packing to receive a signed copy of the new record. This led to extraordinary results, with some areas of the country running out of Beach Nut Gum, and over 38,000 singles being distributed. Sun Records had to purchase an autograph stamp and hire temporary staff to manage the demand, splitting profits with Dick Clark. "The result was extraordinary."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: "Crazy Arms" - Father's Disappointment
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis believed his father, Elmo Lewis, wasn't impressed by "Crazy Arms" because Elmo had always wanted to be a musician but gave up playing piano when young Jerry Lee cried upon seeing his father play a song he himself was struggling with, fearing he would demoralize his son. "Jerry Lee believes to this day that the reason his dad wasn't hugely impressed by Jerry Lee's first record was just that, that seeing his son achieve an ambition he'd given up on himself was at best bittersweet."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: "Ripping" Piano Technique
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis rose to fame using a distinctive piano technique called "ripping," where he would slide his fingers across the keys as fast as possible, often constantly during his solos. The popularity of this style influenced Leonard Chess to insist that Chuck Berry's pianist, Johnny Johnson, adopt it for Berry's recordings. "Lewis tended to use a simple technique called ripping when playing the piano, in which you just slide your fingers across the keys as fast as possible."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 67: "Johnny B. Goode", by Chuck Berry

podcast.title: "The Great I Am" Nickname
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis was known to refer to himself blasphemously as "The Great I Am," reflecting his immense self-belief in his destiny to be a great star. "a man who had been known to refer to himself blasterously as The Great I Am."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Going On" - Inspiration and Adoption
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis adapted "Whole Lotta Shakin' Going On" from Johnny Little John's live performance, which was faster and included a spoken section encouraging the audience to "wiggle around just a little bit." Lewis later admitted to doing it "just like Johnny Duhit" and did not feel guilty, especially as it made women in the audience dance. "I had done it just like Johnny Duhit, maybe I should have felt guilty about that."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Going On" - Recording Anecdotes
podcast.body: While Cowboy Jack Clement claimed the song was recorded in a single take with only three minutes of tape left, the reality involved several takes, with both Clement and Phillips contributing ideas, changing instrumentation, lowering the bass in the mix, and adding slapback echo to the piano, ultimately achieving a spontaneous sound. "There are different stories about the recording of whole lot of shaking going on."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Al Jolson Incident
podcast.body: On a date at the cinema, Lewis heard an Al Jolson song playing before the film, immediately left, cycled home, worked out the song on piano, then cycled back to rejoin his date, claiming he was gone so long because he picked up popcorn. "Lewis immediately got out of his seat, told his girlfriend he needed to use the toilet, cycled home, worked out how to play the song on the piano, cycled back and rejoined his date for the film."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Auditioning for Sun Records
podcast.body: Jerry Lee and his father drove to Memphis, staying in their first hotel with running water after selling hundreds of eggs from their hen house to afford it. When Sam Phillips was out, Jerry Lee refused to leave Sun Studio until someone listened to him, eventually convincing Cowboy Jack Clement to hear him play for three or four hours, making his piano sound "better than Chet Atkins on guitar." "It was now or never, and Jerry Lee was just going to stay there until someone listened to him play the piano."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Career Rebuilding
podcast.body: After the scandal destroyed his career and led to the end of Sam Phillips' reign at Sun Records, Jerry Lee Lewis spent several years struggling to produce hits. He gradually rebuilt his audience by playing small venues and winning over crowds one at a time, paving the way for a comeback in the late 1960s. "Jerry Lee Lewis meanwhile spent several years trying and failing to have a hit, but slowly rebuilding his live audiences, playing small venues and winning back his audience one crowd at a time."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Child Prodigy
podcast.body: At four years old, Jerry Lee felt an urge to play the piano at his rich uncle Lee Calhoun's house and almost instantly figured out "Silent Night." His parents, doting on him after the tragic death of his older brother, recognized his talent and nurtured it; his father even remortgaged his farm to buy Jerry Lee a piano and later wired their house for electricity so he could listen to the radio. "His parents, who always doated on him and tried to give him everything he wanted after the tragically young death of his older brother, realized that they might have a child prodigy on their hands."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Confidence and Arrogance
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis consistently displayed immense confidence and a tendency to show off. He openly challenged Elvis Presley's piano playing and, despite being a relative newcomer with only one single out for days, he naturally took the lead during jam sessions with established stars like Elvis. This "cheeky" character trait was noted as being completely in line with his later career. "Remember at this time, Jerry Lee Lewis was nobody at all, someone who had one single out which had been out a matter of days. But here he is, she wetting with the king of rock and roll, and seeing himself as the person who should naturally be taking the lead."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Disputes on the Alan Freed Tour
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis embarked on a legendary tour with Chuck Berry, Buddy Holly, Larry Williams, The Chantels, and other acts. The tour became renowned not for its music, but for personal disputes between Lewis and Berry. One incident involved Lewis's father, Elmo, who was known for using racial slurs and threatening behavior. After a parking dispute between Lewis and Berry, Elmo chased Berry three blocks with a knife, shouting racial threats, though the next day they were friendly. Another point of contention was Berry's belief that he should headline over Lewis, prompting Lewis to perform increasingly outrageous stunts to upstage Berry, including an apocryphal story of setting his piano on fire during "Great Balls of Fire." "The tour later became legendary, not so much for the music, though that was great, but for the personal disputes between Lewis and Berry."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Divorce from Myra Gale Brown
podcast.body: Around the time of his late 1960s comeback, Myra Gale Brown divorced Jerry Lee Lewis, citing physical and emotional abuse. Myra is now known as Myra Williams, has been happily married for 36 years, and works as a real estate agent. "Mire divorced Jerry Lee around that time, citing physical and emotional abuse."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Duality of Religion and Secular Life
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis was deeply religious and studied at the Southwestern Bible Institute to become a priest, but was expelled for playing a hymn with a boogie feel, which administrators deemed "inciting lust." This tension between religious and secular worlds would persist throughout his life, with him being "firmly on the side of the devil" by the time he signed with Sun Records at age 21. "This tension between religion and the secular world would recur throughout Lewis's life, but by the time he signed to Sun Records, aged 21, he was firmly on the side of the devil."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Early Life Controversies - Marriages
podcast.body: Before his fame, Jerry Lee Lewis had already been married twice, failing to divorce his first wife before marrying the second, and was contemplating leaving his second wife as well. "He'd already got married twice, and hadn't actually got around to divorcing his first wife before marrying the second."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Early Obsession with Music
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis, from Faraday, Louisiana, had an unparalleled obsession with music, driving him to create and giving him vast knowledge across genres, often playing piano for eight hours a day. "Lewis was the one who had the greatest obsession with his music, the greatest drive to create and the greatest sheer knowledge of music in all different genres."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Early Rock and Roll Music
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis's music was directly associated with the rock and roll sound of the 1950s and early 60s, which was a direct descendant of 12-bar blues. This music was characterized by clean, clear guitar sounds and mostly clean lyrics, often intended for kids and played on radio stations appealing to teenagers. "the rock and roll sound became associated and intertwined with the music of the 1950s and early 60s, Elvis, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 3

podcast.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis was a foundational pioneer of rock and roll, counted among the "piano heroes" whose piano playing was central to the genre's initial sound. His style was key in shaping the percussive and energetic rhythm and blues-influenced foundation of early rock. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Piano Heroes

podcast.title: Early Touring with Cash and Perkins
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis toured with Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins, and Wanda Jackson, bringing only whiskey, comic books, and cherry bombs in addition to their clothes and instruments. He quickly rose from the third-billed act to the headliner because "nobody could follow him," leading to resentment from Perkins and Cash, who saw him as Sam Phillips's new golden boy and plotted to leave Sun. "The only things Jerry Lee and his band brought with them on the tour, other than their clothes and instruments, were whiskey, comic books and cherry bombs."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Elvis's Successor
podcast.body: With Elvis Presley about to be drafted into the army, Jerry Lee Lewis saw an opportunity to take over the role of the biggest rock and roll star, intending to become the new "king of rock and roll." "With Elvis about to be drafted into the army, the role of biggest rock and roll star was wide open, and Lewis intended to take over Elvis's mantle."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Extreme Piano Playing and Controversy
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis, a relative of preacher Jimmy Swaggart, was known for his extreme stage antics, which included pounding pianos to splinters and sometimes setting them on fire. His notoriety was further fueled by his controversial marriage to his 13-year-old cousin. "He pounded his pianos to splinters and sometimes set his pianos on fire. And this is before he married his 13 year old cousin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

podcast.title: Impact on Rock's Momentum
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis is cited as one of the key figures whose emergence, alongside Elvis and Little Richard, made rock music unstoppable. Despite widespread criticism, record burnings, and attempts by authorities to crack down on the genre, rock solidified its presence in music following his rise. "None of this actually slowed anything down, of course. We got Elvis, then Little Richard, then Jerry Lee Lewis. And then after that, the Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The More Things Change Part 2

podcast.title: Influence on Harry Webb
podcast.body: Harry Webb (Cliff Richard) had a broad musical taste that included Jerry Lee Lewis, alongside Elvis, even though he also gravitated towards smoother American soft rockers. "Other than Elvis and Jerry Lee Lewis, his tastes ran to smoother American soft rockers, like Vicki Nelson and the Everly Brothers."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: Influence on Rockabilly Instrumentation
podcast.body: The inclusion of instruments like piano or drums in rockabilly music was mainly justified because excluding them would mean overlooking significant artists such as Jerry Lee Lewis, whose piano playing was an integral part of his sound. "You could add a few other elements, like piano or drums, mostly because anything else would exclude Geri Lee Lewis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Initial Interaction with Carl Perkins
podcast.body: After recording "Your True Love," Jerry Lee Lewis bluntly told Carl Perkins that "That song ain't worth a damn." Perkins initially thought Lewis lacked originality, hearing elements of himself, Elvis, and Hank Williams in Lewis's playing and singing of his new record. "He'd got Perkins' backup after they'd finished recording Your True Love, when he'd said, bluntly. That song ain't worth a damn."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Jealousy of Johnny Little John
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis toured with blind musician Paul Whitehead and bassist Johnny Little John, noting Little John's Elvis-like style with jealousy. "Little John had something of the style of Elvis, and Jerry Lee was jealous of him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Judd Phillips' Vision
podcast.body: Sam Phillips' brother, Judd Phillips, who handled much of Sun's promotion, recognized Jerry Lee Lewis's star potential from his appearance and performance, particularly how his slicked-back hair would fall into "wild blonde shocks," and knew he needed to be on TV, specifically the Ed Sullivan or Steve Allen Show. "Judd did a lot of the promotion work for Son and he saw something in Jerry Lee."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Later Marriages and Controversies
podcast.body: Following his divorce from Myra, Jerry Lee Lewis married four more times. His fourth and fifth wives died under mysterious circumstances; the fourth drowned shortly before their divorce was finalized, and the fifth's death remains unclear, with suspicions raised that Lewis may have been involved. In the late 1970s, Lewis, known as "The Killer," shot his bass player in the chest, claiming it was an accident. He was also arrested outside Graceland while drunk and armed, yelling for Elvis Presley to emerge and settle who was the "real king." Lewis is currently 84 years old, married to his seventh wife (who is Myra's brother's ex-wife), still performs, and, according to recent interviews, remains concerned about his eternal fate. "The man known as the killer did once shoot his bass player in the chest in the late 70s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Longevity in Life
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis lived to the age of 87, defying odds in his long life. "Jerry Lee Lewis, who divide all odds by living to the age of 87."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: In Memoriam of Those Lost in 2022

podcast.title: Million Dollar Quartet Participant
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis was present during the famous Million Dollar Quartet sessions when Elvis Presley continually raved about Jackie Wilson, then a singer with Billy Ward and the Dominoes. "In the famous million dollar quartet tapes, you can hear Elvis raving about Wilson to Johnny Cash, Karl Perkins, and Jerry Lee Lewis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Million Dollar Quartet as Career Catalyst
podcast.body: The Million Dollar Quartet session "might well have been the making of Jerry Lee Lewis." Although the recordings were not released until decades later, Sam Phillips used the opportunity for extensive publicity, which positioned Lewis as an equal to Elvis Presley, Carl Perkins, and Johnny Cash, significantly boosting his career. "The million dollar quartet session might well have been the making of Jerry Lee Lewis, even though the recordings weren't released until decades later."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Musical Comparison to George Jones
podcast.body: George Jones's early hit "White Lightning" was noted to sound "a little bit" like Jerry Lee Lewis, placing it closer to early rock and roll. "When I hear that, I hear a little bit of Jerry Lee Lewis."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 2 - Countryish Music of the 1970s (Encore)

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 2 - Countryish Music of the 1970s (Encore)

podcast.title: Musical Influences from Guitarists
podcast.body: Despite being from Louisiana, a hub of great piano playing, Jerry Lee Lewis's main musical influences were guitarists, with Jimmie Rodgers being his favorite musician. "most of his musical influences were guitarists."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Musical Prowess and Influences
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis is described as "one of the most musically-fechland people who ever lived." He was a Louisiana piano player, like Fats Domino, but his biggest influence was Moon Mulligan. He absorbed every piece of music he heard and was eager to perform for people regardless of the song. "Lewis was, by every account I've ever read, one of the most musically-fechland people who ever lived."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Niagara Falls Detour
podcast.body: During a tour, Jerry Lee insisted on a detour to Niagara Falls, got out of the car, stood for 30 seconds, declared, "Jerry Lee Lewis has seen the Niagara Falls, now let's go home boys," and got back in. "Jerry Lee Lewis has seen the Niagara Falls, now let's go home boys."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Pentecostal Upbringing and Rebellion
podcast.body: Raised in a strict Pentecostal family where cinema was a sin, young Jerry Lee would often cause trouble, once dragging his double-first cousin, Jimmy Swaggart, to a movie, causing Swaggart to run out crying, convinced he was damned, while Jerry Lee stayed to watch the cowboys. "As a kid, Jerry Lee was always the one who would get his relatives into trouble."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Pioneering Headbanging-like Movement
podcast.body: In the 1950s, Jerry Lee Lewis developed a signature stage move where he would continuously flip his curls back from his face as they came loose during his energetic performances. Some fans began imitating this movement, which is considered a potential precursor to modern rock headbanging. "The curls on his head would come loose and fall into his face. He had to continuously flip them back so he could see what he was doing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 2

podcast.title: Rejection by RCA and Grand Ole Opry
podcast.body: Before signing with Sun Records, Jerry Lee Lewis tried RCA Records, the label Elvis was on, and the Grand Ole Opry, but was told he needed to play guitar, not piano, to get a chance. "They told him he needed to play a guitar."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Religious Background
podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis was brought up in the Assembly of God, a Pentecostal holy roller church, sharing this religious culture with Elvis Presley. This shared background meant they had more in common religiously than with Johnny Cash or Carl Perkins. "Both Elvis and Jerry Lee were brought up in the assembly of God, a Pentecostal holy roller church, which we'll talk more about when we get to an episode on Jerry Lee himself."

podcast.title: Respect for Chuck Berry
podcast.body: Despite their frequent clashes, Jerry Lee Lewis showed unusual respect for Chuck Berry, partly due to his admiration for Berry's songwriting, going so far as to call Berry "the Hank Williams of Rock and Roll"—the highest praise imaginable from Lewis. Both Jerry Lee and his father, Elmo, were careful to prevent news of their feuds from reaching Lewis's mother, who strongly believed Chuck Berry was "the greatest rock and roller in the world," surpassing even Elvis and her own son. "Partly, that's because of Lewis's admiration for Berry's songwriting. He's called Berry the Hank Williams of Rock and Roll before now, and for someone who had met as Williams as much as Lewis does, that's about the highest imaginable praise."

podcast.title: Sewing Machine Salesman
podcast.body: Prior to his music career taking off, Jerry Lee Lewis made a living as a sewing machine salesman, employing a deceptive tactic of telling women they had won a machine in a contest to con them into buying one on credit. "He'd been making a living as a sewing machine-salesman, conning women into signing up to buy one on credit, by telling them they'd won the machine in a contest."

podcast.title: Steve Allen Show Booking
podcast.body: Judd Phillips took Jerry Lee to New York for a 15-minute meeting with Steve Allen's manager and NBC's head of talent, arriving without usual booking materials while Jerry Lee read a Superman comic and blew bubble gum. Judd persuaded them to let Jerry Lee play, emphasizing that records couldn't capture his performance; his playing so impressed them that they offered $500 to keep him from other shows and booked him for an appearance in a month. "They booked him in for an appearance on the Steve Allen show in a month's time."

podcast.title: Steve Allen Show Performance
podcast.body: During his appearance, Jerry Lee Lewis famously screamed "shake," kicked his piano stool across the stage, which was then thrown back by Steve Allen, the host known for his contempt for rock and roll. This moment launched Jerry Lee Lewis into stardom. "That was the moment when Jerry Lee Lewis became a star."

podcast.title: Theological Discussion with Sam Phillips
podcast.body: While recording "Great Balls of Fire," Jerry Lee Lewis became concerned that the song sounded "satanic," aligning with contemporary criticisms of rock and roll as "the devil's music." This led to an angry, rambling theological discussion with Sam Phillips, which was recorded. The conversation revealed Lewis's deep belief in a physical hell and his conviction that his music would lead him there, showcasing his tortured mindset and making him difficult to work with. Sam Phillips, demonstrating remarkable patience, eventually calmed Lewis down and convinced him to continue recording. "He truly believed in the existence of a physical hell, and that he was destined to go there because of his music."

podcast.body: Jerry Lee Lewis was previously involved in an underage sex scandal, which is referenced in the transcript to provide context for Chuck Berry's similar legal troubles, noting that both were largely forgiven by rock history's narrative. "It's an unfortunate fact of chronology that I have to deal with this, the week after dealing with Gerry Lee Lewis's own underage sex scandal."

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Music
xref.body: Little Richard's music was directly associated with the rock and roll sound of the 1950s and early 60s, which was a direct descendant of 12-bar blues. This music was characterized by clean, clear guitar sounds and mostly clean lyrics, often intended for kids and played on radio stations appealing to teenagers. "the rock and roll sound became associated and intertwined with the music of the 1950s and early 60s, Elvis, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis and so on."

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero
xref.body: Little Richard was an early pioneer of rock and roll, recognized as one of the "piano heroes" who led the genre before the electric guitar became dominant. These pioneers were known for their energetic piano playing, contributing to the "honkin rhythm" that characterized early rock and roll, which evolved from rhythm and blues combos. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero

His contributions helped integrate elements of jazz, boogie-woogie, and barrel house into the emerging rock sound. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."

xref.title: Godmother of Rock and Roll
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe, a queer Black woman from Cotton Plant, Arkansas, is widely called the "Godmother of rock and roll." She was a pioneering guitarist who transitioned to the electric guitar, revered by figures like Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis, Elvis Presley, Little Richard, and Chuck Berry for her influential bridge between gospel blues and swing music. "A lot of people will point to sister Rosetta Thar, a guitarist who graduated to the electric guitar and has been called the Godmother of rock and roll."

xref.title: Impact on Rock's Momentum
xref.body: Elvis is cited as one of the key figures whose emergence, alongside Little Richard and Jerry Lee Lewis, made rock music unstoppable. Despite widespread criticism, record burnings, and attempts by authorities to crack down on the genre, rock solidified its presence in music following his rise. "None of this actually slowed anything down, of course. We got Elvis, then Little Richard, then Jerry Lee Lewis. And then after that, the Beatles."

xref.title: Impact on Rock's Unstoppable Rise
xref.body: The emergence of The Beatles, following Elvis, Little Richard, and Jerry Lee Lewis, cemented rock's status as an unstoppable force. Their success ensured that, despite criticisms from ministers, record burnings, and crackdowns by authorities, rock music would endure. "And then after the Beatles, rock was unstoppable. No matter how many ministers wailed against it, no matter how many records were burned, no matter how many authorities tried to crack down on it, rock was here to stay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The More Things Change Part 2

xref.title: Profound Influence on Blues and Rock Pioneers
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe had a deep impact on the trajectory of the blues and on the pioneers of rock and roll, including major figures like Little Richard, Chuck Berry, Jerry Lee Lewis, and Johnny Cash, all of whom were ardent fans. Her work also captivated British musicians such as Keith Richards, Eric Clapton, and Jeff Beck. "What is not in dispute is that sister Rosetta Tharp had a profound effect on the course of the blues, and then with the pioneers of rock."
